title: Declare signet-3a6a7c's LLO wasm-artifact wait in a local .vigil.toml
description:
Move this repo's cross-repo wait out of vigil's central config and into a
`.vigil.toml` fragment here, so the repo that OWNS the wait declares it.

## Mechanism (already exists, verified in vigil src/config.rs)

vigil's global config carries `repos = [...]`; each adopted directory
contributes its own `[[watches]]` from a `.vigil.toml` at its root.
`load_effective_config` applies per-repo defaults:

    if watch.repo.local_path.is_none() && watch.repo.remote.is_none() {
        watch.repo.local_path = Some(repo_dir.clone());   // only if BOTH unset
    }
    if watch.bead_repo.is_none() && !watch.bead_ids.is_empty() {
        watch.bead_repo = Some(repo_dir.clone());         // this repo's own store
    }

That fits a cross-repo wait exactly: set `repo.remote` explicitly (which
suppresses the local_path default) and `bead_repo` correctly falls back to
THIS repo. Duplicate watch names across sources are refused loudly, naming
both files. Fragments cannot adopt further repos — no recursion.

## Why it is better than the central file

Today vigil's watches.toml would have to know this repo's bead ids. That is
central inference about someone else's state. A fragment is authored by the
repo that actually holds the bead, versioned in ITS history, and moves with
it. Same discipline as the rest of the release-contract work: declare
locally, do not infer centrally.

## Verify before arming

`vigil run --config <path> --dry-run` reads for real (gh, crates.io, the
bead store) and writes nothing. A watch that would act prints
`WOULD notify <bead-id> (<evidence>)`. Check that line names the right bead
and carries evidence you believe before this fragment goes live.

Caveat: `--dry-run` prints `UNCHECKED` for merge_shaped watches. git_pull's
check IS its pull, so a dry run genuinely cannot exercise that path. Only
tool_poll conditions are verified by it.

## Note on on_resolve

Default is `Close`. For a bead that is BLOCKED-class — real work that could
not start until an external fact was true — use `on_resolve = "comment"`.
Closing such a bead destroys the work item rather than completing it. See
vigil-cbbed3: the default is destructive-on-omission and is being changed.

## This repo's watch

signet-3a6a7c waits on ley-line-open v0.14.0's wasm artifacts. AS OF
2026-08-04 THAT CONDITION IS ALREADY TRUE — v0.14.0 published
2026-07-31T05:23:48Z carrying all four declared assets (leyline_sign.wasm,
leyline_cas_ffi.wasm, leyline_envelope.wasm, SHA256SUMS). Verified by
`vigil run --dry-run`, which printed:

    llo v0.14.0 wasm assets: WOULD notify signet-3a6a7c (release v0.14.0
    published 2026-07-31T05:23:48Z carries all 4 declared assets (...))

So signet-3a6a7c has been unblocked for days and nothing said so. The
fragment below is what makes the NEXT one arrive on its own.

    [[watches]]
    name = "signet: llo wasm artifacts"
    bead_ids = ["signet-3a6a7c"]
    on_resolve = "comment"     # blocked-class: lift the blocker, do not close the work
    [watches.repo]
    remote = "agentic-research/ley-line-open"
    [watches.condition]
    type = "release_assets"
    tag = "v0.14.0"
    assets = ["leyline_sign.wasm", "leyline_cas_ffi.wasm", "leyline_envelope.wasm", "SHA256SUMS"]

Source of truth for the shape: vigil tests/fixtures/watches/ley-line-open-v0.14.0.toml.
Requires vigil's global config to list this directory in `repos`.

MIGRATION CORRECTION — read before writing .vigil.toml. Two things in this
bead's original description were wrong or incomplete.

## 1. The two signet paths are ONE directory, not two

    /Users/jamesgardner/github  ->  /Users/jamesgardner/remotes   (symlink, 2025-02-16)

So `github/art/signet` and `remotes/art/signet` are the same directory —
verified, same inode 16777233:123260920. There is no "old path" to migrate
FROM in any meaningful sense, and nothing is currently broken by it. The
notification vigil wrote to signet-3a6a7c on 2026-08-04 landed exactly once
and is readable through either spelling.

Use `/Users/jamesgardner/remotes/art/signet` as the canonical form anyway —
one spelling, consistently — but do not treat this as a data migration.

## 2. The real hazard, which this bead originally set up

vigil's global config currently has:

    name = "llo v0.14.0 wasm assets"
    bead_ids = ["signet-3a6a7c"]
    bead_repo = "/Users/jamesgardner/github/art/signet"

and this bead told you to create:

    name = "signet: llo wasm artifacts"     <- DIFFERENT NAME

Different names means vigil's duplicate-name check does NOT fire. Both
watches act on signet-3a6a7c. `notify_marker` is keyed by watch NAME, so
each writes its own `[vigil:...]` marker, neither sees the other's, neither
reaches its terminal state, and signet-3a6a7c collects a fresh pair of

the same store is now refused at LOAD, with both watch names and the
canonical store path in the message. Paths are canonicalized first, so the
symlink alias cannot hide the collision. Verified against the real config —
before the fix the half-migration loaded cleanly.

So a half-done migration now fails loudly instead of double-notifying. You
still have to do both halves.

1. Create `/Users/jamesgardner/remotes/art/signet/.vigil.toml` with BOTH
   watches — this bead's LLO wasm wait and signet-6da4b0's signature-bundle
   watch. One file, one change; they conflict otherwise.
2. In `~/.config/vigil/watches.toml`, DELETE the watch named exactly
   `llo v0.14.0 wasm assets` (bead_ids = ["signet-3a6a7c"]). Leave
   `llo v0.14.0 wasm assets (notme)` alone — different bead, different store.
3. Add `/Users/jamesgardner/remotes/art/signet` to the top-level `repos`

4. `vigil run --config ~/.config/vigil/watches.toml --dry-run` and read it.

Expected after a correct migration: the signet wasm watch reports
`resolved (beads already notified)` — the marker vigil wrote on 2026-08-04
is still there and still terminal, under the OLD watch name. If you rename
the watch, that marker no longer matches and signet-3a6a7c gets a second

Which is the argument for keeping the name `llo v0.14.0 wasm assets`
verbatim in the fragment rather than the prettier `signet: llo wasm
artifacts` this bead originally suggested. The marker is the terminal state;
renaming the watch resets it.

title: harden: SIG1 payload is parsed twice pre-authentication in DecodeSIG1
description: Found by adversarial review of PR #152 (signet-62f8e0). DecodeSIG1 (pkg/signet/sig1.go) base64-decodes and fully CBOR-parses the payload via Unmarshal BEFORE any signature verification — and as of the layout-boundary fix that is two CBOR parses (the layout probe into map[any]RawMessage plus the struct decode) on attacker-supplied bytes. VerifySIG1 calls DecodeSIG1 first, then verifies. Today this is not a live production surface (no callers outside pkg/signet), which is why it is not a release blocker, but it becomes one the moment SIG1 is wired into a network path. Options to evaluate: cap the accepted payload size before decoding; verify the COSE signature before the token decode (requires restructuring since the verifier needs the payload bytes, not the parsed token — the bytes are available pre-parse); or document the parse-before-verify ordering as intentional with an explicit input bound. Do not close by asserting 'not exploitable today' — pick a bound or an ordering.
acceptance_criteria: Either the SIG1 decode path enforces an explicit maximum payload size before CBOR parsing, or signature verification precedes token parsing; a test covers the chosen bound/ordering with an oversized or unsigned payload; the decision is recorded in docs/design/001-signet-tokens.md.

title: ci: go-version pins are stale and rely on implicit toolchain auto-download

- rig Worker TS wrapper designed (rig-959350)

comments.text:
## Discovery: `leyline-sign` crate already exists

`ley-line/rs/crates/sign/` (`leyline-sign` v0.1.0) implements the Rust CMS/PKCS#7 + Ed25519 signing primitives that this ADR proposes. 12 tests pass.

### What's already built:
- **`cms.rs`** (~870 lines) — Full CMS/PKCS#7 SignedData creation + verification (RFC 5652 + RFC 8419). Both signed-attributes and PureEdDSA modes. DER encode/parse from scratch (mirrors go-cms). Weak algorithm rejection (MD5/SHA-1). Constant-time digest comparison.
- **`cert.rs`** — X.509 cert parsing (via `x509-cert` crate), signer identifier extraction, key-match verification.
- **`ffi.rs`** — C FFI (`leyline_sign_data`, `leyline_sign_data_without_attributes`, `leyline_verify`) with buffer-based API. Builds as cdylib + staticlib + rlib.
- **`oid.rs`** — OID constants (id-data, id-signedData, SHA-512, Ed25519, CMS attributes).
- **`error.rs`** — Typed errors (`SignError`, `VerifyError`).
- **`cbindgen.toml`** — C header generation configured.

### Deps (all pure Rust / RustCrypto — Wasm-compatible):
`cms 0.2`, `der 0.7`, `x509-cert 0.2`, `spki 0.7`, `const-oid 0.9`, `ed25519-dalek 2.1`, `sha2 0.10`

### What's missing vs this ADR:
1. **Bridge cert issuance** — signet's `pkg/attest/x509/` (short-lived certs from OIDC claims). Not in leyline-sign.
2. **OIDC JWT validation** — signet's `pkg/oidc/`. Not in leyline-sign.
3. **Capability extensions** — ASN.1 custom extensions for MCP capabilities. Not in leyline-sign.
4. **Wasm build target** — deps are Wasm-compatible but no `wasm32-wasi` target tested yet.
5. **Git signing CLI** — README mentions gpgsm-compatible binary for jj, but no `main.rs` binary yet (only lib).

### Recommendation:
Rename scope of this bead. `leyline-sign` IS the signet-core signing layer. What's needed is:
- Add bridge cert issuance to `leyline-sign` (or a sibling `leyline-attest` crate)
- Add OIDC validation (or a sibling `leyline-oidc` crate) 
- Test wasm32-wasi compilation
- Wire signet Go code to call leyline-sign via FFI (cdylib) or replace go-cms entirely
comments.author: rsry-mcp

comments.text:
## Rescoping: this is not "rewrite signet in Rust" — it's "split signet along runtime boundaries"

### Discovery (2026-03-23)
- `leyline-sign` (Rust, 276KB Wasm) already covers Ed25519 + CMS/PKCS#7 — the ONLY custom crypto
- `rig-959350` (closed) proved the CF Worker path: Wasm for signing, TS for OIDC/JWT (WebCrypto)
- Go signet authority works fine on Fly/k8s — no reason to replace it

### The real question: what's the split?

Signet today is a single Go binary serving multiple deployment targets that have fundamentally different runtime constraints:

| Runtime | What runs there | Constraints |
|---------|----------------|-------------|
| **CF Worker** (Wasm) | Ed25519 sign/verify, CMS, cert exchange | No filesystem, no long processes, 128MB mem, must be Wasm |
| **CF Worker** (TS) | OIDC JWT validation, session mgmt, DO state | WebCrypto covers JWT, no custom crypto needed |
| **k8s / Fly** (Go) | Full authority server, OIDC provider registry, policy eval, rate limiting, CA | Needs filesystem (keys), long-running process, full stdlib |
| **CLI** (Go) | `signet sign`, `signet auth login`, `signet-git` | Needs OS access, keystore, browser launch |

Go is basically required for k8s/Fly (ecosystem, tooling, existing infra). Wasm is required for CF edge. These aren't competing — they serve different tiers.

### Proposed split (not a rewrite):
1. **signet** (Go, unchanged) — authority server + CLI + k8s operator. The "control plane."
2. **leyline-sign** (Rust→Wasm) — crypto primitives at edge. Already exists, 276KB.
3. **TS glue in rig** — OIDC + session + DO. Calls leyline-sign Wasm for signing. Calls signet authority for full cert chain validation when needed.

### What this bead should become:
NOT "ADR: signet-core in Rust/Wasm" but rather "ADR: signet runtime split — which operations belong at which tier?" The crypto is solved. The architecture question is: which signet authority endpoints can be served entirely at the edge (Wasm+TS) vs which need the full Go server behind a tunnel?

Candidates for edge-only (no Go roundtrip):
- Certificate exchange (Ed25519 sign → Wasm, OIDC verify → WebCrypto)
- Health check
- Landing page (already done — static HTML via rig Dockerfile)

Must stay on Go server:
- Full CA operations (key generation, cert chain management)
- PKCS#11 integration
- Policy evaluation with complex rules
- Rate limiting with persistent state (unless DO handles it)
comments.author: rsry-mcp

title: master_sk adopts URL-spec resolver (align with cloister ADR-0014 v2)
description:
## What

Adopt the same URL-spec resolver pattern cloister uses for `VAULT_KEK_SOURCE`. Signet's master_sk loader should accept:

- `keychain://<service>` (macOS)
- `secret-tool://<service>` (Linux libsecret)
- `file:///path/to/key.pem` (any platform, including CI)
- `env://VAR` (today: plaintext; future: age-encrypted ciphertext)
- `http(s)://helper/...` (generic helper)

## Why

title: Shared trust-anchor-helper protocol (factor out cloister's kek-helper.mjs)
description:
## What

Generalize cloister's `kek-helper.mjs` sidecar into a shared trust-anchor-helper that both cloister's vault DO AND signet's master_sk loader consume. Same binary, same wire protocol.

## Why

- cloister vault needs OS-keystore access (workerd can't shell to `security` / `secret-tool` directly — V8 isolate)
- signet master_sk loader needs the same OS-keystore access — adopting URL-spec resolver
- Without sharing, both repos implement keychain://+secret-tool:// resolution twice and risk divergence

## Wire protocol (proposed)

JSON-over-stdio OR JSON-over-Unix-socket OR HTTP-on-loopback. Cloister's current `kek-helper.mjs` uses HTTP-on-loopback:

```
GET /resolve?url=keychain://com.notme/master
  200 OK
  Content-Type: application/octet-stream
  <raw bytes>

GET /resolve?url=keychain://does-not-exist
  404 Not Found
  Content-Type: application/json
  {"error":"not_found"}
```

For signing operations (where the helper holds the key and signs on behalf of caller — better than `resolve` for long-term keys):

```
POST /sign
  Body: {"url":"keychain://com.notme/master","alg":"ed25519","message_b64":"..."}
  Response: {"ok":true,"signature_b64":"..."}
```

`op: sign` is strongly preferred over `op: resolve` for the master_sk path — the key never leaves the helper, only signatures cross the wire.

## Mirror of

[cloister-12b062](https://github.com/agentic-research/cloister) — the cross-repo bead in cloister's store.

## Implementation options

1. **Standalone repo** (`trust-anchor-helper` / `tah`) — both cloister and signet depend on it via release artifact
2. **In signet's tree** (`cmd/trust-anchor-helper/`) — signet owns the binary, cloister consumes
3. **In each repo with shared SPEC.md** — duplication but no cross-repo coupling

Lean toward option 2 (signet owns it) because:
- signet's domain IS trust roots / signing
- Go is the right language (talks to OS Security framework / libsecret natively)
- cloister's kek-helper.mjs becomes a thin Node port-of-protocol for cases where the Go binary isn't appropriate

## Suggested files

- `cmd/trust-anchor-helper/main.go` (new)
- `pkg/keystore/keychain_darwin.go`
- `pkg/keystore/libsecret_linux.go`
- `pkg/keystore/file.go`
- `docs/trust-anchor-helper-spec.md` (canonical protocol spec)
- `Taskfile.yml` / Makefile — build target

## Done when

- One binary, two consumers (cloister vault DO, signet master_sk loader)
- Protocol spec'd in `docs/trust-anchor-helper-spec.md`
- Both `op: resolve` (returns bytes) AND `op: sign` (key stays in helper) implemented
- macOS Keychain + Linux libsecret + file:// all working
- cloister's `scripts/kek-helper.mjs` deprecated with a pointer at this binary
- cloister's tests pass against the new helper (vitest stub remains identical because the wire is the same)

## Coordinated with

- signet master_sk URL-spec adoption (sibling bead in signet)
- cloister-127a3c / cloister-12b062 (cloister-side coordination)
- cloister-125199 (already shipped — cloister's vault now requires the resolver)

title: Define the canonical protocol-kid derivation + emit pinned cross-language test vectors (trust-root authority)
description:
Signet owns the canonical `kid` that binds a signed Σ head / bridge cert / JWK to a resolvable Ed25519 public key. Today three repos derive `kid` three incompatible ways, so no verifier can resolve an LLO head's `signerKid` against notme's JWKS:

- LLO (Rust):   BLAKE3(raw 32-byte Ed25519 pubkey)[..8]      — 64 bits
- notme (TS):   RFC-7638-ish truncated SHA-256 over SPKI DER — 64 bits
- signet (Go):  generateSubjectKeyID = SHA-1 over raw/SPKI   — 160 bits (X.509 SubjectKeyId)

DECISION (locked with @jamestexas 2026-07-21):
- Canonical derivation = `BLAKE3(raw 32-byte Ed25519 public key)`, truncated to 128 bits (16 bytes). BLAKE3 keeps LLO scoped to a single hash — the one intentional Σ seam. Raw key (not SPKI DER) removes encoding ambiguity across languages. 128 bits (not LLO's current 64) so a trust-root-adversary can't lean on ~2^32 birthday cost even though kid is selection-not-authorization.
- Hash choice is safe because JWK `kid` is opaque per RFC 7517 §4.5 — notme's own consumers opaque-match (`keys.find(k => k.kid === header.kid)`, worker.js:37085), never recompute RFC-7638. Cloudflare Access sits UPSTREAM of notme (notme verifies CF JWTs), so nobody external recomputes notme's kid. Verified 2026-07-21.
- signet's existing SHA-1 `generateSubjectKeyID` STAYS as the X.509 SubjectKeyId cert field (RFC 5280 §4.2.1.2) — a separate concern, untouched.

Deliverables:
1. ADR in signet/docs/ defining the canonical kid (hash, input encoding, width, versioning — a change is v2, not an edit).
2. `Kid(ed25519.PublicKey) []byte` (or similar) in signet/pkg, plus its inverse discipline (kid is not reversible; document that it selects, never authorizes).
3. A pinned vector fixture (JSON or capnp) shipping known (pubkey -> kid) pairs, committed to signet and consumed by LLO/notme/cloister CI. leyline-net/v1 pinned-bytes discipline: changing a vector is a breaking protocol event.

Close condition: `cd ~/remotes/art/signet && go test ./pkg/... -run Kid` green AND the vector fixture file exists and is referenced by the ADR.

title: MCP transport security via signet HTTP middleware
description:
## Problem

MCP (Model Context Protocol) has no authentication story. Tool calls over HTTP
are unsigned JSON-RPC — any client can invoke any tool with no proof of identity.

## Proposal

Use signet's existing HTTP middleware (`pkg/http/middleware`) to sign/verify
MCP tool calls over the streamable HTTP transport:

1. **Sign tool calls** — agent signs each `tools/call` request with an ephemeral
   cert. MCP server verifies proof-of-possession.
2. **Sign tool results** — server signs responses so agents can verify provenance.
3. **Wrap mache serve** — signet middleware around `mache serve --http` endpoint.

stdio transport doesn't need this (same trust boundary — subprocess).

## Prior Art

- signet already has `middleware.SignetMiddleware` with clock skew, master key verification
- ley-line ADR-004 planned signet for manifest signing — same pattern applies to MCP
- MCP spec has no auth section; this would be a novel contribution

## Files

- pkg/http/middleware/ (existing middleware)
- New: pkg/mcp/ or integration in mache's serve.go

title: sigstore-kms-signet has no CI-usable key path — the only options in Actions are worse than keyless
description:
## Problem

`cmd/sigstore-kms-signet` is a real Sigstore KMS plugin (implements `kms.SignerVerifier` via `signature/kms/cliplugin/handler`), so `cosign sign --key signet://default` produces a standard cosign signature — the object supply-chain scanners actually count. That makes it the natural way for repos in this org to sign artifacts under a signet-rooted identity instead of an ephemeral Fulcio one.

It is not reachable from GitHub Actions without making key handling worse. The plugin loads from OS keyring or `~/.signet/master.key` (`cmd/sigstore-kms-signet/main.go` header). Neither exists on a runner, so a consumer has exactly two options:

1. **Put `SIGNET_MASTER_KEY` in GitHub secrets.** This is the posture `gha-identity.yml`'s own header says that workflow exists to eliminate — verbatim: *"notme.bot → bridge cert pair (eliminates SIGNET_MASTER_KEY in GH)"*. Adopting the plugin this way would undo the thing the identity workflow was built for.

2. **Use the notme.bot bridge Ed25519 signing cert.** No secret, but the same header states private keys *"never leave the action process memory by design"* and consumers *"must instead invoke the action in the same job/step where the keys are used."* That constraint does not compose with a matrix build that produces artifacts in one job and signs in another — which is the shape of most release workflows, including this repo's.

## Evidence that the gap is real rather than theoretical

`signet`'s own `release.yml:134` signs with **keyless** cosign (`cosign sign-blob --yes`, Fulcio OIDC via `sigstore/cosign-installer`), not with `signet://`. The repo does not dogfood its own plugin in CI. That is the strongest available signal that no CI-shaped path currently exists.

## Why this is being filed now

ley-line-open is closing `ley-line-open-9abefd` (LLO publishes unsigned OCI images — provenance attestation is attached via `attest-build-provenance` with `push-to-registry: true`, but there is no cosign-format image signature, which is what scanners count as "signed"). signet was the preferred signer. On investigation LLO is going with keyless cosign for now, because it needs no secret and matches what signet chose for itself. `--key signet://default` is a drop-in swap for the keyless flags later, so nothing is foreclosed — but the swap is not currently possible.

This is a report from a consumer, not a claim on signet's roadmap. The framing may be wrong; the observation is that there is no documented middle path between "keyless" and "master key as a repo secret."

## Possible shapes (signet's call, not the reporter's)

- A companion reusable workflow to `gha-identity.yml` that exposes signing itself, so the same-step key constraint is satisfied *inside* signet's workflow and consumers pass in a digest and get a signature back.
- A KMS plugin mode that accepts a bridge cert / short-lived key from the notme.bot exchange rather than requiring keyring or master key on disk.
- An explicit docs statement that CI signing is keyless-only by design and `signet://` is a workstation-scope trust root — which would also be a complete resolution, and would have answered this in ten seconds.

## References

- `cmd/sigstore-kms-signet/main.go` — key loading, `signet://<key-id>` URI scheme
- `.github/workflows/gha-identity.yml` — `workflow_call`, bridge cert pair, the two constraints quoted above
- `.github/workflows/release.yml:69,84-89,134` — keyless signing in practice
- `docs/sigstore-integration.md` — documents `sign-blob --key signet://default` (workstation flow)
- Consumer: `ley-line-open-9abefd`

title: Least-privilege GitHub token scoping for agent onboarding
description:
Current GH token has way too many permissions: delete repos, full control of private repos, update workflows, create gists, full SSH key control. An agent getting onboarded via signet auth register should need MUCH less.

Minimum viable scopes for an agent:
- repo (read) — to clone and read code
- contents (write) — to push commits to branches
- pull_requests (write) — to create PRs
- NO: delete repos, admin, SSH keys, gists, workflows, org management

This is the onboarding flow:
1. Human authenticates via OAuth (needs broader scopes)
2. Human requests bridge cert for agent (POST /api/cert/bootstrap)
3. Agent uses bridge cert for mTLS — no GH token needed for MCP access
4. Agent needs a SEPARATE, scoped GH token ONLY for git push/PR creation

Design questions:
- Should signet mint a GitHub App installation token (scoped per-repo) instead of using the human's PAT?
- Should the bridge cert itself carry repo scope claims that the orchestrator enforces?
- How does this relate to the CF for SaaS design (rig-0c27c2)?

Related: PR agentic-research/signet#108 (agent-scoped certs), notme.bot/architecture (auth flow docs)

title: Cap'n Proto schemas for cross-language type parity (CABundle, GHAClaims, APAS predicates)
description:
CRITICAL: TypeScript signs CABundles with JSON + alphabetical key sort. Go signs with CBOR canonical encoding. These produce different byte sequences — cross-language verification will fail silently.

Cap'n Proto solves this: deterministic binary format, identical bytes across TS/Go/Rust from same .capnp schema. ley-line already uses capnp (rs/ll/net/schema/manifest.capnp).

Types that need .capnp definitions:
1. CABundle (revocation) — epoch, seqno, keys, keyId, signature
2. TokenClaims (revocation check) — keyId, epoch
3. GitHubActionsClaims (OIDC) — 12+ fields, TS uses Zod, Go uses struct
4. BridgeCertResult — certificate PEM, expires_at, subject
5. APAS predicates — DispatchDefinition, RunDetails, Handoff (from rosary)
6. RevocationReason — enum (epoch_mismatch, unknown_key, rollback_attack, bundle_invalid, bundle_stale)

Ecosystem: capnp-ts for TS (needs CF Workers compat testing), go-capnproto2 for Go (mature), capnpc-rust for Rust (mature). ley-line already has working capnp in Rust.

title: Watch the next signet release for its signature bundles — signing is merged but has never run
description:
The secretless signing path is MERGED AND UNPROVEN. Nothing has exercised it,
and the first thing that does will be a real release. This bead is the watch
that reports whether it worked, on the first run, without anyone remembering
to look.

## State, measured 2026-08-04

    latest release   v0.2.1, 2026-03-22
    its assets       checksums-sha256.txt, signet-darwin-arm64,
                     signet-linux-amd64, signet-linux-arm64
                     -> no .sigstore.json, no .pem, nothing attesting
    unreleased       57 commits since v0.2.1
    signing landed   TODAY: 24e9d1e (signet-9b0ecd), 8af4e08 (signet-579491)

So `release.yml` now signs and verifies, and the newest published release
predates that by four months. The next tag is the first execution of this
code in anger.

## Exact assets to watch for — read from source, not guessed

`cmd/sigstore-kms-signet/sign_artifact.go:29-36` (`artifactOutputPaths`)
emits four files per artifact:

    <artifact>.sigstore.json     bundle
    <artifact>.signet.crt.pem    leaf cert
    <artifact>.signet.ca.pem     CA bundle
    <artifact>.signet.pub        ephemeral public key

`release.yml` signs four inputs: signet-darwin-arm64, signet-linux-amd64,
signet-linux-arm64, checksums-sha256.txt. So a complete release carries
4 binaries/checksums + 16 signing artifacts + the originals.

Do NOT hand-type these into the watch from this bead. Re-read
`artifactOutputPaths` when you write it — if the suffixes have changed, the
watch must change with them, and a stale asset name produces a watch that
waits forever while reporting a calm "not yet". That failure mode is the
whole reason this bead spells out where the names live rather than just
listing them.

## The watch

Add to `.vigil.toml` at this repo root (see signet-0e0a6b, which introduces
that file for the LLO wasm wait — do both in one change):

    [[watches]]
    name = "signet: next release is signed"
    bead_ids = []              # observation only; writes to no bead store
    [watches.repo]
    remote = "agentic-research/signet"
    [watches.condition]
    type = "release_assets"
    tag = "<the next tag>"
    assets = [
      "signet-linux-amd64.sigstore.json",
      "signet-darwin-arm64.sigstore.json",
      "signet-linux-arm64.sigstore.json",
      "checksums-sha256.txt.sigstore.json",
    ]

`release_assets` is deliberate and not interchangeable with `release_tag`: a
tag can exist and the release be published while the signing step failed or
its assets never uploaded. That distinction is the condition entire reason
for existing. `bead_ids = []` means no `on_resolve` is needed and nothing is
written anywhere — it observes and prints.

Verify before arming: `vigil run --config <path> --dry-run`. It reads for
real and writes nothing.

## Why this is worth a P1 rather than being left to notice later

signet is the identity component — signet-9b0ecd own words: its binaries are
what other systems here trust to establish identity. Two failure modes are
both silent from outside:

1. Signing breaks and the release ships unsigned. `release.yml` verifies
   what it signed BEFORE creating the release, which should turn this into a
   failed run rather than a bad release — but that guard has never fired in
   production either, so it is a design claim, not an observed one.
2. Signing works and nobody confirms it, so the first person to actually
   check is whoever is investigating an incident.

## Related, and the reason this pattern matters beyond signet

This repo just solved, correctly, a problem vigil spent 2026-08-04 working
around. `fence_report` (vigil-2aadea) reads egress-enforcement evidence out
of a GitHub JOB LOG, which GitHub expires — see openai/fence#154. Signet
publishes its evidence as RELEASE ASSETS: durable, publicly fetchable, and
checkable by a condition vigil already had. Producer-published evidence beats
observer-scraped evidence, and this is the working example.

Contrast worth keeping in view: ley-line-open-a03156 — LLO release workflow
is green for v0.15.0 and v0.15.1 while publishing no crates at all (crates.io
still at 0.14.0, `cargo publish` appears nowhere in that repo). Green release,
missing surface, nothing reporting it. Same class of hole this watch closes
for signet.

PR #146 reviewed. The fragment is correct — and one line in it is a guess
worth knowing about before the fragment gets REGISTERED (it is inert until
then, so this is not a merge blocker).

## Correct, confirmed against source

- `name = "llo v0.14.0 wasm assets"` kept verbatim, with a comment saying
  why. That is what stops signet-3a6a7c getting a second comment: the
  notify marker is keyed by watch name and the existing marker is the
  terminal state.
- `bead_repo` omitted — right. load_effective_config defaults it to the
  adopted dir when bead_ids is non-empty, i.e. signet's own store.
- `[watches.repo] remote = ...` set explicitly, which suppresses the
  local_path default. Correct for a cross-repo wait.
- Second watch has `bead_ids = []`, so no on_resolve is needed. Correct.
- `.sigstore.json` suffixes match cmd/sigstore-kms-signet/sign_artifact.go
  `artifactOutputPaths`, not the workflow's prose. Correct.

## The guess: tag = "v0.2.2"

signet is at v0.2.1 with 57 unreleased commits, and 8af4e08 is
`feat(sigstore): add secretless CI artifact signing`. Under semver a feat
bumps the MINOR — v0.3.0 is at least as likely as v0.2.2, and pre-1.0
practice in this ecosystem has been minor-bumps-for-features (LLO went
0.13 -> 0.14 -> 0.15 on feature releases).

If signet cuts v0.3.0, this watch reports `not yet (release v0.2.2 not
found (not cut yet?))` forever. It will look healthy. Nothing distinguishes
"waiting for a release that has not happened" from "waiting for a release
that will never happen because the version was guessed wrong" — the watch
becomes unfalsifiable, which is the failure mode this repo's own §6.0 rule
exists to prevent, pointed at itself.

## Mitigations, in order of preference

1. WAIT to register this fragment until signet's next tag is actually cut,
   then set the real version. Costs nothing; the fragment is inert.
2. Set the tag at release time as part of cutting it — the release PR
   updates .vigil.toml in the same change that bumps the version.
3. Blocked on vigil: there is no "latest release" condition. Every vigil
   condition names an exact tag, so every fragment is one release from
   silently stale. `latest_release_assets` would make "the NEXT release,
   whatever it is called, carries these bundles" expressible — which is what
   this watch actually means. `gh release view` with no tag argument already
   returns the latest, and it can reuse interpret_release_assets with the
   evidence naming the tag observed. Tracked against vigil-11d5c0, which
   raised the same version-churn problem for fragments generally.

Recommend (1) now and (3) as the durable fix.

## Unrelated, verified while here: vigil-267f8c has no portability problem

The concern that `.github/actions/sign-artifact` builds from signet's own
source does not bite a consuming repo. The action installs Go itself
(`go-version-file: ${{ github.action_path }}/../../../go.mod`), and GitHub
checks out the WHOLE repo for a remote composite action, so
`cd $SIGNET_ACTION_PATH/../../..` lands on signet's root with cmd/ present.
A Rust repo can consume it with no Go setup of its own.

The `/exchange-token` endpoint verifies GHA OIDC tokens and maps capabilities, but the actual bridge certificate minting is still TODO (authority.go:1097-1108). This means the full flow — ambient GHA OIDC identity → bridge cert → artifact/commit signing — cannot be exercised end-to-end in CI yet.

- `cmd/signet/authority.go` — authority server with `/exchange-token` endpoint (token exchange works, cert minting is stubbed)

GHA OIDC is the most practical path to "signet in the cloud" — no secrets to manage, ambient identity from the CI platform, short-lived certs that match signet's security model.

title: Epic: GHA OIDC end-to-end signing flow
description:
## Overview

Enable the full flow: GHA ambient OIDC token → Signet authority → bridge cert with capabilities → signed artifacts — with no secrets stored in the repo.

## ADR Convergence

This epic sits at the intersection of four ADRs:
- **004** (Bridge Certs): Capability-bearing X.509 extensions, the cert format
- **007** (Progressive Identity): Level 3 = enterprise OIDC, bridge cert in identity hierarchy
- **008** (Pluggable Signers): `crypto.Signer` interface enables cloud KMS for authority master key
- **011** (Policy Bundles): Controls who gets certs and what capabilities — currently "anyone with valid OIDC token" (§2)

## The Flow

```
GHA Workflow → ambient OIDC JWT (no secrets)
  → POST /exchange-token to Signet Authority
  → Authority validates token (pkg/oidc/)
  → Policy evaluation: allowed repos/workflows/capabilities (ADR-011)
  → Mint bridge cert with capability X.509 extensions (ADR-004)
  → Signed by authority master key (ADR-008 signer backend)
  → Workflow uses bridge cert to sign artifacts
  → Verification by relying party
```

## Sub-beads

1. Bridge cert with capability X.509 extensions (pkg/attest/x509/)
2. Policy evaluation interface for OIDC subjects (pkg/policy/)
3. Complete bridge cert minting in authority /exchange-token
4. CLI: `signet authority exchange-github-token`
5. GHA workflow: OIDC signing e2e test
6. Git signing with external bridge cert (ADR-007 Level 3)

## Notes

- ADR-008's crypto.Signer is already in LocalCA — cloud KMS just works with no code change. Future bead for KMS backend.
- ADR-011 MVP: existing AllowedRepositories/AllowedWorkflows config IS the policy. Full SCIM bundles are a later epic.
- Authority can run ephemerally in GHA workflow for testing (no cloud deployment needed initially).

title: Bridge cert with capability X.509 extensions
description:
## What

Create `IssueBridgeCertificate()` in `pkg/attest/x509/bridge.go` that mints X.509 certificates with capability URIs embedded as extensions per ADR-004.

## Why

The `/exchange-token` endpoint verifies OIDC tokens and maps capabilities but cannot mint bridge certs (authority.go:1097 is TODO). This bead provides the cert-minting primitive.

## Design (from ADR-004)

X.509 extension with signet OID containing:
```asn1
SignetCapabilityAttestation ::= SEQUENCE {
  version      INTEGER DEFAULT 1,
  capabilities SEQUENCE OF UTF8String,
  audience     SEQUENCE OF UTF8String,
  notAfter     GeneralizedTime OPTIONAL,
}
```

Capability URIs follow: `urn:signet:cap:{action}:{resource}[:{constraint}*]`

The bridge cert is an intermediate CA (`IsCA: true, MaxPathLen: 0`) so it can issue ephemeral certs for actual signing — same pattern as ADR-007 Level 1+.

## Implementation

- New function `IssueBridgeCertificate(ephemeralPubKey, capabilities []string, validity time.Duration) (*x509.Certificate, []byte, error)` on `LocalCA`
- Uses `ExtraExtensions` on the X.509 template for capability attestation
- OID: `1.3.6.1.4.1.99999.1.3` (next in existing signet private OID arc)
- Capabilities encoded as ASN.1 SEQUENCE OF UTF8String
- Cert subject: `CN=signet-bridge, O=Signet`
- Returns cert + DER bytes

## Acceptance

- Unit tests for: valid capability encoding, empty caps, round-trip (encode→parse→verify), cert chain validation (bridge signs ephemeral)
- Verify the issued cert's extension can be parsed back to capability URIs

title: Policy evaluation interface for OIDC subjects
description:
## What

Create a policy evaluation interface in `pkg/policy/evaluator.go` that determines whether an OIDC subject is allowed to receive a bridge cert and what capabilities they should get.

## Why

ADR-011 §2: "The authority currently issues certificates to anyone with a valid OIDC token. There is no organizational policy layer." The existing `AllowedRepositories`/`AllowedWorkflows` in `GitHubActionsConfig` is hardcoded config — not a composable interface the authority can call.

## Design

```go
// PolicyEvaluator determines authorization for OIDC subjects.
type PolicyEvaluator interface {
    // Evaluate checks if a subject is allowed and returns granted capabilities.
    Evaluate(ctx context.Context, req *EvaluationRequest) (*EvaluationResult, error)
}

type EvaluationRequest struct {
    Provider   string                 // "github-actions"
    Subject    string                 // OIDC sub claim
    Claims     map[string]interface{} // Provider-specific claims
    RequestedCaps []string            // Capabilities requested (optional)
}

type EvaluationResult struct {
    Allowed      bool
    Capabilities []string  // Granted capability URIs
    Validity     time.Duration // Cert validity override (optional)
    Reason       string    // Denial reason (for logging)
}
```

MVP implementation: `StaticPolicyEvaluator` that wraps the existing `AllowedRepositories`/`AllowedWorkflows`/`MapCapabilities` logic from `pkg/oidc/github.go`. This is a refactor, not new policy logic.

Future: `BundlePolicyEvaluator` that evaluates signed policy bundles per ADR-011.

## Acceptance

- Interface defined with clear contract
- StaticPolicyEvaluator passes tests for: allowed repo, denied repo, allowed workflow, denied workflow, empty allowlists (allow all), capability mapping delegation to provider
- Authority can be configured with a PolicyEvaluator (consumed in bead 3)

title: Complete bridge cert minting in authority /exchange-token
description:
## What

## Why

The `/exchange-token` endpoint currently verifies tokens, maps capabilities, but returns JSON with capabilities and no cert. This is the glue that connects OIDC verification → policy evaluation → bridge cert minting → PEM response.

```json
{"status": "success", "capabilities": [...]}
```

to:
```json
{"status": "success", "capabilities": [...], "certificate": "-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----\n..."}
```

- Bead signet-882eca (bridge cert minting primitive)
- Bead for policy evaluator interface

## Acceptance

- Integration test: mock OIDC token → exchange → receive valid PEM cert
- Cert contains capability extensions that round-trip correctly
- Cert is signed by authority master key
- Cert's ephemeral public key matches the one sent in the request
- Error cases: invalid token, denied by policy, malformed ephemeral key

title: CLI: signet authority exchange-github-token
description:
## What

Create a CLI command that a GHA workflow can call to exchange its ambient OIDC token for a Signet bridge certificate.

## Why

The example workflow in `docs/examples/github-actions-workflow.yml` references `signet authority exchange-github-token` which doesn't exist. CI needs a simple CLI interface, not raw curl.

## Design

New file `cmd/signet/authority_exchange.go` with Cobra command added as child of `authorityCmd` via `init()`:

```
signet authority exchange-github-token \
  --authority-url https://signet-authority.example.com \
  --token "$GITHUB_OIDC_TOKEN" \
  --output ~/.signet/bridge-cert.pem
```

Or with ambient detection (auto-reads `ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_URL`/`ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_TOKEN`):

```
signet authority exchange-github-token \
  --authority-url https://signet-authority.example.com \
  --auto \
  --output ~/.signet/bridge-cert.pem
```

Flow:
1. If `--auto`: fetch OIDC token from GHA environment
2. Generate ephemeral Ed25519 keypair locally
3. POST to `{authority-url}/exchange-token` with token + ephemeral pub key
4. Receive bridge cert PEM
5. Save cert + ephemeral private key to output path(s)

## Acceptance

- `--auto` mode reads GHA env vars and requests OIDC token with correct audience
- `--token` mode accepts explicit token string
- Ephemeral key generated securely, saved alongside cert
- Error messages are clear for: authority unreachable, token rejected, invalid response

description:
## What

Enable signet-git to use an externally-provided bridge cert (from OIDC exchange) in the signing chain, implementing ADR-007 Level 3.

## Why

ADR-007 Level 3: `signet-git init --oidc https://company.okta.com` — bridge cert comes from external OIDC provider. For GHA: the bridge cert from `/exchange-token` should slot into the git signing chain as: authority master key → bridge cert → ephemeral cert → commit signature.

## Design

New `pkg/git/identity.go`:
```go
type Identity struct {
    MasterKey  *keys.Ed25519Signer  // Machine identity (always present)
    MachineID  string
    UserEmail  string               // Optional (Level 1+)
    BridgeCert *x509.Certificate    // Optional (Level 1+)
    BridgeKey  *keys.SecurePrivateKey
}

func (i *Identity) Level() int { ... }
func (i *Identity) HasUserAttribution() bool { ... }
func LoadIdentity(cfg *config.Config) (*Identity, error) { ... }
```

Updated signing flow in `pkg/git/sign.go`:
- If bridge cert present: master → bridge → ephemeral → commit (3-cert chain)
- If not: master → ephemeral → commit (existing 2-cert chain)

CMS signature includes bridge cert in intermediate chain via `cms.SignOptions{IntermediateCerts: [bridgeCert]}`.

## Stretch goal

This is independent of the authority beads — it's about the client-side cert chain. Can be worked in parallel with beads 1-2.

## Acceptance

- Level 0 signing unchanged (backward compatible)
- Level 1+ signing produces CMS with bridge cert in chain
- git log --show-signature works with bridge cert chain
- Integration test in Docker verifies both Level 0 and Level 1+ paths

title: GitHub Release binaries ship unsigned — no cosign anywhere in the repo
description:
Found 2026-08-04 during a cross-repo supply-chain sweep from notme. Verified against this tree.

FINDING: .github/workflows publishes release artifacts via softprops/action-gh-release, and there is NO cosign anywhere in the repo — `grep -rl cosign .github/workflows/ Taskfile.yml` returns zero files. Release binaries are downloadable with nothing attesting where they came from.

WHY THIS ONE IS SHARPER THAN THE CONTAINER CASE: signet is the identity server. Its binaries are what other systems in this ecosystem trust to establish identity — notme's own docs point at signet for the APAS spec and bridge-cert protocol. An unsigned binary from the identity component is the worst artifact in the set to leave unattested, because a consumer has no way to distinguish a real release from one uploaded by anyone who obtained release-write access.

The repo already grants `id-token: write` in 6 places, so the OIDC identity that keyless signing requires is present and in use. The gap is the signing itself, not the plumbing.

WHAT TO DO — binaries, not images, so it is `cosign sign-blob` rather than `cosign sign`:

1. `cosign sign-blob --yes --bundle <artifact>.cosign.bundle <artifact>` for each published binary, and upload the bundle alongside it. The bundle form keeps the signature, cert and Rekor entry in one file the consumer fetches next to the artifact.
2. VERIFY IMMEDIATELY AFTER SIGNING, in the same job, with `cosign verify-blob --bundle` against `https://github.com/${GITHUB_WORKFLOW_REF}` as an EXACT identity, not a regex. A signature nothing checks is indistinguishable from one that silently did not happen — notme shipped three npm releases whose `--provenance` flag was a no-op for exactly that reason (notme-77ead7), and notme's own images were signed-but-never-verified until PR #65.
3. Document the consumer command with the identity pinned to the release WORKFLOW, not just the repo. notme's published command used `^https://github.com/agentic-research/notme/` with no terminator, which matched ANY workflow in the repo — so any workflow holding `id-token: write` could produce a signature that passed it.

Also worth considering here specifically: SLSA provenance via actions/attest-build-provenance, since consumers of an identity binary have more reason than most to want the build inputs attested and not only the output signed.

See notme docs/design/016-signing-surfaces.md and notme PR #65 for the working reference.

NOT proposed as a shared GitHub Action from notme, deliberately: a verify step supplied by another repo means a mistake or compromise there silently neuters the check everywhere it is used, and the check exists to catch precisely that. Independent duplication is correct for verifiers.

comments.text:
PR #144 opened — https://github.com/agentic-research/signet/pull/144

Implemented against the acceptance criteria:

- **Every published artifact gets a cosign bundle.** `release.yml` signs each `signet-*` binary plus `checksums-sha256.txt` with `cosign sign-blob --bundle`. Bundles land in `release-assets/`, which `files: release-assets/*` already globs, so they upload alongside.
- **Verified in the same job.** `cosign verify-blob --bundle` runs per artifact immediately after signing, against `--certificate-identity "https://github.com/${GITHUB_WORKFLOW_REF}"` (exact, not regex) and `--certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com`.
- **Release fails if verification fails.** Confirmed by execution, not inspection: tampered blob → cosign exit 1; the `set -euo pipefail` loop aborts on it; the `Create GitHub Release` step never runs.
- **Consumer instructions pin the workflow, not the repo.** New README "From a Release" section — the repo previously documented no release-binary install path at all. Identity is `.../.github/workflows/release.yml@refs/tags/$VERSION`, with an explicit note that loosening to a repo-level regexp lets any workflow holding `id-token: write` satisfy the check.

Two things worth recording beyond the criteria:

1. The `release` job had `permissions: contents: write` only. `id-token: write` had to be added — keyless signing was not previously possible from that job even if someone had tried.
2. First draft's empty-artifact guard was `artifacts=(signet-* checksums-sha256.txt)` checked for length 0. `nullglob` drops an unmatched glob but not a literal, so with zero binaries the array is length 1 — the guard could never fire while reading as a safety net. Same shape as the fixture fixed-point problem in notme's ADR-016 rule 7: a check that passes by construction. Now guards the `signet-*` glob specifically; both branches tested.

cosign pinned to v3.1.1 (the installer's default is v3.0.6) so CI runs the exact version the round-trip was exercised against.

Leaving open until #144 merges.
comments.author: rsry-mcp

comments.text:
Merged as `24e9d1e` (PR #144, squash). All four checks green: Pure Go, PKCS#11+CGO, Security Checks, Performance Benchmarks.

**Verification record.** The signing step only runs on tag pushes, so PR CI does not exercise it. Rather than leave that unproven, the `run:` block was extracted verbatim from the committed workflow and executed locally against fake artifacts, with a shim translating the keyless flags to key-based ones (cosign v3.1.1 — the version now pinned in the workflow):

| Case | Result |
|---|---|
| 3 binaries + checksums | 4 bundles written, all `Verified OK`; the `signet-*` glob expands before the loop so bundles are not re-signed |
| Binary substituted after signing | `invalid signature`, exit 1, loop aborts before the remaining artifact — release step unreachable |
| Zero binaries in `release-assets` | guard fires, exit 1 |

One caveat worth recording: the first tamper run "passed" for the wrong reason — `cd` clobbered `$OLDPWD`, so the shim failed on a missing key file rather than a signature mismatch, and still exited 1. Rewritten with absolute key paths plus a clean-run sanity assertion (must exit 0) before the tamper case, so a shim breakage cannot be mistaken for a caught tamper. Same failure class as ADR-016 rule 7 — a check that passes by construction proves nothing.

The next tagged release is the first real end-to-end exercise; if Fulcio/Rekor behave differently than the key-mode shim, the release fails loudly at the verify step rather than publishing unsigned, which is the correct failure direction.

title: Keystore UX: rename --insecure → --keystore-backend, expose ephemeral mode for testing/CI
description:
## What

`signet-git init` writes to the OS keyring (Keychain on macOS, Secret Service on Linux) by default and has no clean way to materialize an ephemeral/test keystore without `--insecure`. The flag is misnamed for the actual use case.

## Concrete UX gap

```
$ signet-git init --home $TMPDIR/signet-test
initialization failed: master key already exists in keyring (use --force to overwrite)
```

- `--home` is silently ignored — keyring is global per-user, no namespacing
- The only "isolated" path is `--insecure`, which clobbers home `master.key` with no auth, BUT in a tmpdir+chmod-600 file it is **not** less secure than a shared system keyring — it is just *different*
- `--insecure` framing actively discourages the path that should be the canonical test/CI mode
- No `--keystore=ephemeral` or `--keystore=memory` mode for true throwaway keys

## Why this matters

1. **Testability**: cannot dogfood `signet-git` sign→verify roundtrip in CI without either (a) clobbering the developer's real master key with `--force`, or (b) following the `--insecure` path which the help text actively warns against.
2. **Integration tests**: `scripts/testing/test_integration.sh` runs in Docker (no keyring), so it already takes the `--insecure` path implicitly. The naming makes the test path look like a hack.
3. **CI on macOS/Linux runners**: keyring access in headless runners is flaky (Linux requires dbus + gnome-keyring; macOS Keychain needs unlock). The current default-to-keyring + opt-out-via-`--insecure` design forces every CI workflow to know about the workaround.

## Proposed design (sketch — needs ADR-level decision)

**Option A: Rename + reframe**
```
signet-git init                                # auto-detect: keyring if available, else file
signet-git init --keystore=keyring             # explicit keyring
signet-git init --keystore=file --home <path>  # explicit file (replaces --insecure)
signet-git init --keystore=ephemeral           # tmpfs, never persisted
```
Deprecate `--insecure` (keep as hidden alias for one release).

**Option B: Namespaced keyring**
Allow `--service-name=signet-test-XXXX` to namespace within the keyring. Solves test isolation without leaving the secure backend. More invasive — needs keyring entry-cleanup story.

**Option C: Hybrid**
- `--home` always wins (when set, force file-based regardless of keyring availability)
- Rename `--insecure` → `--file-keystore` or just remove the flag in favor of `--home`-implies-file

## Acceptance criteria

- A new contributor can run a sign→verify roundtrip against signet-git from a fresh clone without touching their real keyring
- `scripts/testing/test_integration.sh` no longer needs to pass `--insecure` (the flag is gone or the path is the documented default for test contexts)
- The help text for the chosen flag does not describe the test path as "insecure"

## Discovered by

Dogfooding PR #126 (pkg/git unit tests). User flag: "we need to actually use the code and not trust tests only" — the immediate friction was that there's no clean way to run signet-git against an ephemeral keystore.

## Out of scope

- Hardware-backed keystores (Touch ID signer, PKCS#11) — those are different backends, tracked separately
- The keyring service-name collision question (signet vs notme on the same machine) — separate concern

## Files likely touched

- `cmd/signet-git/init.go` (or wherever the init subcommand lives)
- `pkg/cli/keystore/secure.go`
- `pkg/cli/keystore/insecure.go` (if it exists; if not, the file-based loader)
- Help text + README pointers
- Possibly an ADR in `docs/design/` if the change is breaking

comments.text:
**Additional finding from dogfooding PR #126:**

Even with `signet-git init --home <isolated> --insecure` succeeding (writes `master.key` to the isolated home), subsequent `signet-git export-key-id --home <isolated>` returns the user's **real** keyring KID, not the isolated home's KID.

Root cause: `pkg/cli/keystore` load-priority is hardcoded as **keyring first, file fallback**:

```go
// pkg/git/verify.go:withMasterKeyForVerify (mirrors sign path)
masterKey, err := keystore.LoadMasterKeySecure()        // always tries keyring first
if err != nil {
    // SECURITY: Validate home path before using it for file-based key loading
    masterKey, err = keystore.LoadMasterKeyInsecure(cfg.Home)
}
```

So `--home` is functionally a fallback path — it only takes effect when the keyring is **unavailable** (Docker, headless CI). On a developer's local machine where signet has ever been initialized into the keyring, every subsequent `signet-git` call against any `--home` will load the keyring's master key, not the home's `master.key`.

**Consequences:**

1. The current dogfood workaround (init isolated home with `--insecure`, then sign/verify against it) does **not** actually use the isolated key — it uses the user's real master key. The signing/verify code paths *are* exercised end-to-end (PR #126 dogfooded successfully and produced a valid CMS signature), but the test does not actually isolate from the user's real identity.

2. `scripts/testing/test_integration.sh` runs in Docker (no keyring), so it accidentally takes the file path correctly. But any developer running the integration test locally would silently sign against their real keyring key.

3. The CLI surface implies `--home` selects the keystore; the implementation does not.

**Add to the design:** the `--keystore=file|keyring|ephemeral` option needs to be an **override**, not a hint. When `--keystore=file` is passed (or `--home` is explicitly set in a future cleaner design), the keyring must be skipped entirely — both for read AND write paths. Otherwise the "isolated test" abstraction is a lie.

Files touched would expand to include `pkg/cli/keystore/secure.go` (the load function) and every call site of `LoadMasterKeySecure()` that should respect a keystore-backend override.
comments.author: rsry-mcp

comments.text:
**Update 2026-05-19 — user suggests XDG-based design (simpler than the original `--keystore=` flag proposal)**

Standard Unix convention beats a new flag. The fix:

```
XDG_CONFIG_HOME=$(mktemp -d) signet-git init   # writes there, no keyring touch
XDG_RUNTIME_DIR=$(mktemp -d) signet-git init   # ephemeral (tmpfs on Linux)
```

Every CI runner and integration-test harness already understands XDG; tools like `gh`, `gpg`, `gnupg-modern`, `pass` all respect it. No new flag, no new mental model.

## But XDG alone isn't the whole fix

The dogfooding finding (additional comment on this bead) showed that even with `--home /tmp/...` set, `LoadMasterKeySecure()` hits the OS keyring **first** regardless of the home path. XDG_CONFIG_HOME would have the same problem: it'd direct *writes* to the XDG path but *reads* would still try the keyring first.

The complete fix needs two parts:

1. **Path routing (XDG)** — when `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` is set, use `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/signet/` as the keystore root for both writes (init) and reads (load).
2. **Load-priority routing** — when an XDG path is set OR an explicit file path exists, file beats keyring (or keyring is skipped entirely). Otherwise current keyring-first behavior is preserved.

Concretely, `pkg/cli/keystore/secure.go:LoadMasterKeySecure` and every caller need to either:
- (a) accept a `KeystoreSource` enum (`file | keyring | auto`), defaulting to auto with XDG-implies-file, or
- (b) check for `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/signet/master.key` and short-circuit before the keyring lookup.

(b) is the minimum-viable change.

## Acceptance criteria (updated)

- `XDG_CONFIG_HOME=$(mktemp -d) signet-git init` writes `master.key` to that path and **does not** touch the OS keyring
- `XDG_CONFIG_HOME=$(mktemp -d) signet-git export-key-id` returns the KID for the XDG-home key, **not** the user's real keyring key
- `scripts/testing/test_integration.sh` can drop the `--insecure` flag entirely (or the flag is deprecated → no-op)
- Help text no longer describes the test path as "insecure"
- Backwards compat: when XDG vars are unset, current keyring-first behavior is preserved bit-for-bit

## What this drops from the original proposal

- The `--keystore=file|keyring|ephemeral` flag. XDG covers `file` and `ephemeral` (via `XDG_RUNTIME_DIR`); keyring is the unset-default.
- Custom service-name namespacing inside the keyring (the "Option B" in the original). Not needed if XDG handles isolation.

## What stays

- `--insecure` flag rename/deprecation. Eventually a no-op once XDG handles the test path.
- Audit of `LoadMasterKeySecure()` call sites — every read path needs the same load-priority logic.

title: gha-identity.yml is a diverged local copy of notme's — reconcile or consume the original
description:
signet-resign.yml:34 calls `uses: ./.github/workflows/gha-identity.yml` — a LOCAL copy, not agentic-research/notme's. The two have already diverged: notme's exposes `notme_token` and `expires_in` outputs that signet's does not, and their audience descriptions differ. signet's copy even self-references `agentic-research/signet/...` in its own usage example.

Both implement the same exchange — one GHA OIDC token becomes an octo-sts-scoped GitHub App token plus a notme bridge cert — and both ultimately call the same live service at auth.notme.bot. signet's exists to eliminate SIGNET_MASTER_KEY; notme's to eliminate stored PATs. Same idea, two hand-maintained implementations, already drifting.

WHY THIS IS WORTH TRACKING RATHER THAN SHRUGGING AT. It is another instance of the pattern catalogued in vigil's release-contract design (docs/superpowers/specs/2026-07-27-release-contract-design.md sections 1.2 and 8.1): one good idea implemented independently in several repos, with no shared source, drifting quietly. The others found so far are post-publish verification (LLO, mache), tag-manifest version gating (LLO, mache, canonical-hours, notme), and regen-diff drift gating (LLO, cloister, rosary). This is the identity-primitive instance, and it is the most security-sensitive of them, since divergence in an auth exchange is not a cosmetic difference.

Note the direction of dependency: notme is the TS live auth service implementing the model; signet is the Go client. So signet consuming notme's reusable workflow (`uses: agentic-research/notme/.github/workflows/gha-identity.yml@<sha>`) is the natural shape, not the reverse. notme is private, so verify a private repo's reusable workflow is callable from signet before committing to that direction — if it is not, the fallback is a documented sync with a drift check, in the idiom cloister's generated-drift.yml and rosary's taskfile-contract already establish.

Decide: consume notme's directly, or keep a local copy with an explicit drift gate and a comment saying why. What should not persist is an undeclared copy that silently diverges.

title: signet auth login: support browser-initiated keypair + bridge cert flow
description:
signet auth login works great as a CLI tool (localhost callback, PKCE, auto-configure Claude Code). But the same flow needs to work from a browser context too — for users who hit /sign-in on rosary.bot.

**Current CLI flow (working):**
1. Generate ECDSA P-256 keypair locally
2. Start localhost:random/callback server
3. Open browser → rosary.bot/oauth/authorize → Clerk
4. Receive code at callback, exchange for token
5. POST pubkey to /api/cert, get bridge cert
6. Save cert+key to ~/.signet/mcp/rosary/

**Needed browser flow:**
1. Browser generates keypair via WebCrypto (P-256 or Ed25519)
2. User authenticates via Clerk (already on /sign-in)
3. Browser POSTs pubkey to /api/cert/bootstrap (authenticated via Clerk session)
4. Receives signed bridge cert
5. User downloads cert+key bundle (or we offer `signet auth import` to pull from server)

**Key question:** How does the browser-generated private key get to the user's machine for CLI use? Options:
- Download as .pem file (simple, user copies to ~/.signet/mcp/)
- `signet auth import --from-browser` fetches cert from a short-lived KV slot
- QR code / deep link that signet CLI catches

This connects to sigid: once user has bridge cert, sigid extracts identity claims from it. The cert is the root of trust — everything else is derived.

title: Design: cert-as-root-of-trust — what claims go in X.509 vs sigid CBOR fields
description:
Core architectural question: the bridge cert is the "door key" — proof you're authenticated. Everything else should be derivable. But WHERE do the derived claims live?

**Option A: Claims in X.509 extensions**
- Embed sigid context (provenance, boundary, environment) as X.509 v3 extensions in the bridge cert
- Pro: CF WAF can evaluate extensions at edge, no second lookup
- Con: cert is immutable once issued, can't update claims without reissuing
- Con: X.509 extension OIDs need registration, tooling is painful

**Option B: Claims alongside cert (sigid's current approach)**
- Bridge cert identifies the user (CN=user-{id}, pubkey binding)
- sigid fields (CBOR 20-23) travel in the PoP token, not the cert
- Pro: claims can vary per-request (different boundary for different endpoints)
- Pro: cert stays simple, sigid is the flexible layer
- Con: need both cert AND token for full context

**Option C: Hybrid — minimal claims in cert, rich claims in sigid**
- Cert carries: user ID, issuer, tier (stable claims)
- sigid carries: boundary, environment, delegation chain (dynamic claims)
- ley-line uses cert identity to look up arena permissions
- rosary uses sigid context for dispatch authorization

The connection to ley-line: ley-line manifests are already signed with Ed25519. If the user's bridge cert identity matches ley-line arena permissions, that's the authorization chain: signet cert → sigid context → ley-line access.

Depends on: sigid environment/boundary implementation (fields 21-22, currently stubbed)

comments.text: Decided on Option C (hybrid) during session. Cert carries stable identity (owner, issuer, issuance time via OID 99999.1.{1,2}). sigid carries dynamic context (boundary, environment, delegation) via CBOR fields 20-23. Implemented in PRs #97-#101. This bead is now a documentation task — write the formal ADR.

title: CABundle wire-format divergence: pick canonical-bytes encoding (CBOR-only or JSON-only) and deprecate the other
description:
## Carved off from signet-683223 (closed in PR #128)

The discoverability part of signet-683223 shipped in `docs/design/cross-language-schema.md`. The remaining functional bug is this bead.

## What

`CABundle` is signed in two cryptographically non-interoperable ways across the signet ecosystem:

- **Go (`pkg/revocation/checker.go:168-188`):** canonical CBOR per RFC 8949 §4.2, integer-keyed map
- **TypeScript clients (per the original signet-683223 body):** JSON with alphabetical key sort

These produce different byte sequences over identical logical content, so a `CABundle` signed in one language fails verification silently in the other. Schema-parity in `notme/schema/identity.capnp` does not resolve this — schema parity ≠ wire-format parity.

## Acceptance criteria

- Pick one canonical wire format; update `docs/design/cross-language-schema.md` "Open contract gap (deferred)" callout
- Deprecate or remove the losing format with a stated cutover window
- Add a cross-language test vector (preferably `notme/schema/test-vectors/cabundle/`) proving identical bytes in Go + TypeScript
- Both verifiers reject the deprecated format (or accept it during cutover with a log entry)

## Why this is hard

- JSON+alphabetical-sort is fragile (nested-object key ordering, floats, whitespace); CBOR §4.2 is more battle-tested
- Need to inventory which side has production consumers before deciding which to deprecate
- Cutover affects every existing signed bundle in the losing format

## Discovered by

Body of signet-683223 (P0, closed 2026-05-19). Discoverability part shipped in PR #128 (commit 5f80794); this remaining functional gap was explicitly deferred per "nothing functional ideally" direction.

comments.text:
**Related: signet-2f6b68** (capnp-ify MasterKeyDescriptor)

Per user observation 2026-05-19: both beads are the same architectural hole — **the capnp schema carries types but not canonical bytes**. Together:

- **This bead (bdaf24):** type IS in schema, signed two ways. Pick one canonical encoding.
- **Sibling (2f6b68):** type is NOT in schema, lives signet-side only. Promote it in.

**Combined fix shape:** add a canonical-bytes annotation to `identity.capnp` (e.g. `$canonicalEncoding("cbor-rfc8949-deterministic")`) as part of resolving bdaf24. Then any subsequent promotion (2f6b68 and others) inherits the wire-format contract by virtue of being in the schema. This makes the schema-bridge the single source of truth for *both* shape and bytes, which is the whole point of having a schema.

**Sequencing recommendation:** bdaf24 first (pick + annotate) → schema-bridge ADR formalizes the canonical-bytes convention → 2f6b68 promotes `MasterKeyDescriptor` under it.

title: chore(sign): drop rs/crates/sign fork, depend on LLO's leyline-sign
description:
Signet-side of `ley-line-open-d4fdf4`. Delete signet's leyline-sign fork; consume LLO's canonical version instead.

## Findings

Overlap detector 2026-07-09 confirmed `signet/rs/crates/sign/` is a stale fork of LLO's `leyline-sign`:
- `cert.rs`, `oid.rs` — md5 IDENTICAL to LLO's copies
- `cms.rs` — older subset; adds `signingTime` attribute (LLO deliberately omits for wasm32 time-source portability)
- `ffi.rs` — LLO's copy adds wasm32 allocator exports
- `lib.rs`, `error.rs` — LLO adds cert_chain.rs (901 LoC), bin/helper.rs, host/ (ADR-0019)

Per README (`rs/crates/sign/README.md` ~L9): "Prepared — not yet integrated. Cloudflare Workers currently use `@peculiar/x509` in TypeScript." No Go callers of `signet-sign` (grep on pkg/ finds no imports).

## What ships

### 1. Delete `rs/crates/sign/` entirely

Direct analog of cloister PR #119 (bead `cloister-8f4d3f`, merged 2026-07-09).

### 2. Decide `signingTime` reconciliation

Signet's cms.rs adds signingTime; LLO's omits it. Two paths:

- **A**: LLO adds an optional `signing-time` feature to its leyline-sign; signet consumers enable it if needed. Requires an LLO PR first; then signet's future consumers set `features = ["signing-time"]`.
- **B**: Accept the drop. No signet-issued CMS blobs are in production per README, so no wire compat concern today.

Recommend **B** for this PR since no production consumer exists. If a future signet CMS consumer needs signingTime, refile as path A.

### 3. If signet's Rust workspace becomes empty

`rs/Cargo.toml`'s `members` list drops to zero. Options:
- Delete the whole `rs/` directory (it becomes vestigial)
- Move to `rs.retired/` with a README explaining
- Leave the workspace empty as a placeholder for future Rust work

Agent decides based on whether anything else in signet references the workspace.

### 4. Taskfile cleanup

Remove any `rs:sign:*` targets that referenced the deleted crate.

### 5. Docs update

If any signet docs reference the local crate path, update to point at LLO's `leyline-sign` (git dep or, later, published wasm artifact via LLO bead `ley-line-open-a2099a`).

## Rules

- Commit prefix `[<this-bead-id>]` (Golden Rule 11)
- Signet's local gate (`task check` or equivalent) must be green
- Verify NO Go code imports break (`grep -rn "signet-sign" pkg/`)
- Working copy: `~/remotes/art/signet` (per overlap agent, `~/github/art/signet` and `~/remotes/art/signet` are identical trees)

## Non-goals

- **NO changes to signet's Go tree** (pkg/*, SIG1/COSE, ML-DSA-44 — all genuinely distinct scope)
- **NO wasm-consumer wiring** — that waits on LLO bead `a2099a` (wasm publish infra)
- **NO signingTime feature-gate in LLO** unless path A is chosen (this PR chooses B)

## Related

- `ley-line-open-d4fdf4` — LLO-side tracking + rationale
- `ley-line-open-7226e3` / `cloister-8f4d3f` — cloister analog (reference implementation)
- `ley-line-open-a2099a` — wasm publish infra (blocks future signet-uses-LLO-wasm)

## Provenance

- Overlap detector 2026-07-09
- Cloister consolidation PR #160 landed same day (2026-07-09)

title: P3: extract APAS spec to its own repo (apas-spec) when external implementations appear
description:
Trigger-based, not a current task.

## Current state

`signet/docs/apas/agent-provenance-standard.md` is the APAS spec, currently at v0.2.0-draft (committed 2026-05-09). It lives in signet because:

- signet IS the protocol authority for the cryptographic primitives APAS uses (CBOR canonical, Ed25519, sigid 4-entity model).
- Relative paths from `docs/apas/` to `signet/pkg/...` and `signet/docs/design/...` work natively.
- Single author, single primary consumer (notme), still draft status.

## When to extract

Extract to a dedicated `apas-spec` repo when ANY of these triggers fire:

1. **A second implementation appears** (Go-only, Rust-only, or external) and asks "where's the spec?"
2. **External auditors / partners** want a stable canonical URL for the standard.
3. **Versioned spec releases** become a need (independent of signet's release cadence).
4. **CycloneDX / in-toto / SLSA registries** want to link to APAS as an attestation-format peer.

None are true today.

## Migration plan (when triggered)

1. `git filter-branch` or `git subtree split` the `docs/apas/` history into a new repo `agentic-research/apas-spec`.
2. Move all internal references in signet, notme, rosary, ley-line-open from `signet/docs/apas/...` to `apas-spec/...`.
3. Add a stub `signet/docs/apas/README.md` redirecting to the new repo.
4. Update notme.bot's `/apas` page to render from the new repo.
5. Set up release tags (`v0.2.0`, etc.) on the new repo.
6. Optional: an `apas-spec` GitHub org or `agentic-research/apas` for community contributions.

## Anchors

- `signet/docs/apas/agent-provenance-standard.md` — current home (v0.2.0-draft)
- `signet/docs/apas/research.md` — sibling research doc
- `notme.bot/public/apas.html` — public face (eventually points at the spec repo)
- Conversation 2026-05-09 — extraction trigger discussion

title: release.yml: v0.3.0 (no hyphen) never actually publishes as a prerelease
description:
Found during adversarial review of the Goal Zero release promotion plan (docs/release/goal-zero-promotion.md, bead signet-cf2adc / PR #148).

.github/workflows/release.yml:125 sets `prerelease: ${{ contains(env.TAG, '-') }}`. The plan's Phase 2 (§2) requires tagging `v0.3.0` (no hyphen) and having it "published as prerelease (the beta channel)" for the soak, then flipped at Phase 3 via `gh release edit v0.3.0 --prerelease=false --latest`.

But `contains("v0.3.0", "-")` is false — there is no hyphen in "v0.3.0" — so release.yml will create it with `prerelease: false` from the very first Phase 2 run. It is never actually a GitHub prerelease during the 5-day soak; it's a normal (non-prerelease, just non-"latest") release visible to anyone browsing releases, undermining the "beta channel" framing the whole plan depends on. The plan's own §1 findings section correctly states only hyphenated tags become prereleases — directly contradicting §2 Phase 2's claim two sections later, and invalidating the Phase 3 rollback text "v0.3.0 stays prerelease forever" (it was never prerelease to begin with).

Secondary issue in the same diff: `make_latest: "false"` is unconditional (not just for the first release), so every future production tag (v0.3.1, v0.4.0, ...) will require the same manual `gh release edit --latest` step forever. The plan documents the manual flip only as a one-time "first signed release" asymmetry (§2 Phase 3, parenthetical "this asymmetry disappears after the first signed production release"), not as a permanent behavior now baked into the workflow.

Fix direction: either give the beta tag a real hyphenated form (e.g. v0.3.0-beta.1) promoted in place at Phase 3, or drop the prerelease-flag framing for Phase 2 and rely purely on the latest-pointer for soak isolation — and update the plan to state make_latest=false requires a manual flip on every future release, not only the first.

Plan §1/§2/§5 rewritten to match: the "Pre-release" badge is the channel marker, the soak is intentionally public, and the flip requirement is documented as permanent for all future releases (forgetting it leaves a loud, visible badge — not a silent state). The AC's first two clauses are satisfied; the final clause (gh api shows prerelease:true during soak) is runtime evidence that can only exist once the train runs — it will be captured by signet-ddb0f3 (first live confirmation on the rc) and signet-ddd7d7 (soak), so this bead is linked as a dependency of the soak bead and should close on that observation.

title: verify_release.sh: unanchored identity regexp + silent-pass on malformed checksums
description:
Found during adversarial review of the Goal Zero release promotion plan (docs/release/goal-zero-promotion.md, bead signet-cf2adc / PR #148), reviewing scripts/release/verify_release.sh committed in 2655404.

(a) Weaker identity check than the signing side it claims to mirror. Lines 140-141 use `--certificate-identity-regexp "$IDENTITY_REGEXP"` with default `IDENTITY_REGEXP="agentic-research/signet"` (no `^`/`$` anchors). The signing side (cmd/sigstore-kms-signet/sign_artifact.go:194-208, cosignVerifyBlobArgs) uses exact-match `--certificate-identity <identity>`, not a regex at all. An unanchored regex matches that substring anywhere in the certificate's SAN — any identity string that merely *contains* "agentic-research/signet" would also verify successfully. This contradicts the script's own header comment (lines 27-28): "mirrors cmd/sigstore-kms-signet/sign_artifact.go cosignVerifyBlobArgs." Fix: anchor the default (`^...$`) or switch to `--certificate-identity` with the exact expected identity string.

(b) Silent pass on malformed/empty checksums file. Lines 98-102 build the `artifacts` array purely by parsing `checksums-sha256.txt` with no assertion on the resulting count or the expected artifact set (the 4 known binaries + the checksums file itself). If that file is ever empty or its line format changes, the loop silently produces zero or too few entries, and the script still prints "PASS: ... N artifacts ... verified" for whatever small N it found instead of hard-failing. Fix: assert the parsed artifact count/set against an expected minimum before declaring PASS.

Neither issue is caught by any existing test — there is no test file for verify_release.sh and it isn't invoked from any CI workflow (confirmed via grep); it's a purely human-run gate, so these defects would only surface via a human's own vigilance, not a red build.

comments.text: Fixed on goal-zero/signet-release-plan (PR #148). (1) Identity: default regexp is now anchored — (^|[/:])agentic-research/signet([/:@.]|$) — so the repo path must appear as a path segment, and a new --identity flag does exact --certificate-identity matching for once the enrolled SAN shape is known from a real release; the header comment no longer claims to "mirror" cosignVerifyBlobArgs and instead documents the deliberate exact-vs-regexp relaxation. (2) Silent pass: the script now hard-fails when checksums-sha256.txt names fewer than 3 binaries (release.yml matrix floor) or any non-signet-* artifact name. Verified per the AC by manual runs with a gh shim serving a fixture release: truncated checksums (1 artifact, valid sha) → exit 1 "names only 1 artifacts"; empty checksums → exit 1 "names only 0 artifacts"; flag-shaped tag (--repo) rejected before any network call. Real-release regression check: v0.2.1 still passes checksums then hard-fails naming the four missing bundles. shellcheck clean.
comments.author: rsry-mcp

acceptance_criteria: --certificate-identity-regexp default is anchored (or replaced with exact --certificate-identity match), and the script hard-fails (non-zero exit) when the parsed artifact list from checksums-sha256.txt is empty or below an expected minimum count, verified by a manual run against a release with an intentionally truncated checksums file.

title: Add CF Access as OIDC provider: unified identity → bridge cert flow
description:
CF Access can act as a generic OIDC provider (SaaS app mode). Signet already has a pluggable provider registry. Adding CF Access as a provider means:

1. CF Access authenticates user (Google, GitHub, Okta, OTP — whatever methods configured)
2. CF Access issues OIDC JWT
3. Signet validates JWT (CF Access = another provider alongside GitHub Actions, Clerk)
4. Signet mints bridge cert binding user's key to CF Access-verified identity

Two birds: CF Access handles login UX + session management, signet handles crypto + cert issuance. No redundant auth layers.

Config addition to authority.json:
```json
{"name": "cf-access", "issuer": "https://<team>.cloudflareaccess.com/cdn-cgi/access/certs"}
```

CF Access free tier: 50 users, includes OIDC. No additional cost.

This is a signet change (provider config), not rig. The provider registry code already handles generic OIDC — just needs CF Access JWKS endpoint configured.

Ref: https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/applications/http-apps/saas-apps/generic-oidc-saas/
